summary: Profiles X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for use on the Internet. It was replaced by RFC 5280.

eli5.summary: Certificates are like digital ID cards. This sets the rules for the cards used on the Internet. It has been replaced by RFC 5280.

questions: what is the internet x509 pki profile
what is in an x509 certificate
how does certification path validation work
subtitle: The Internet profile of X.509 v3 certificates and v2 revocation lists, plus how to validate a certification path.

tldr.problem: X.509 is broad, so independent implementations cannot reliably interoperate on the Internet unless they agree on which certificate fields, extensions and checks to use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3280 profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and X.509 v2 CRL for Internet use, defines which extensions are required, adds two Internet-specific extensions, and specifies a certification path validation algorithm.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 2459 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5280, which is the current profile.

facts.label: UTCTime year rule
facts.value: YY of 50 or more is 19YY; less than 50 is 20YY

today: RFC 3280 has been obsoleted by RFC 5280, which is the Internet PKI profile to follow now. It was also updated by RFC 4325 and RFC 4630, and it itself obsoleted RFC 2459.

sections.title: An Internet PKI Profile
sections.content:
RFC 3280 is one part of a family of standards for the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) for the Internet. It profiles the format and meaning of certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs) so that applications such as WWW, electronic mail, user authentication and IPsec can use X.509 in an interoperable way. The profiles are written in the 1988 ASN.1 syntax.

The architecture has end entities, certification authorities (CAs), optional registration authorities (RAs) and CRL issuers, and a repository that stores and distributes certificates and CRLs. A certificate binds a public key to a subject, and the binding is asserted when a trusted CA digitally signs it. Because signature and validity can be checked independently, certificates can be handed around through untrusted servers.

Unlike the rigid hierarchy of the older PEM design in RFC 1422, this profile lets a path start at a CA in the user's own domain or at the top of a hierarchy. X.509 v3 extensions for certificate policies and constraints replace the need for PEM's policy CAs and name subordination rule. Compared with RFC 2459, it adds a detailed path validation algorithm (section 6.1), a CRL-based status algorithm (section 6.3), more detail on delta CRLs, and three new certificate extensions: subject info access, inhibit any-policy and freshest CRL. Key and signature encoding moved to a companion specification.
sections.eli5: Everyone needs to read ID cards the same way. This note says what an Internet ID card looks like and who is allowed to hand them out.

sections.title: Basic Certificate Fields
sections.content:
A certificate is a Certificate made of a to-be-signed part (tbsCertificate), a signature algorithm and the signature value. Signed data is encoded with the ASN.1 distinguished encoding rules (DER). The signed part holds:

  • a version, which MUST be 3 (value 2) when extensions are used, and implementations MUST recognize version 3;
  • a serial number, a positive integer that MUST be unique per CA. Users MUST handle values up to 20 octets and CAs MUST NOT use longer ones;
  • the signature algorithm, which MUST match the outer signatureAlgorithm;
  • an issuer and a subject name, where the issuer MUST be a non-empty distinguished name;
  • a validity period with notBefore and notAfter;
  • the subject public key information, optional unique identifiers, and optional extensions.

Dates through the year 2049 MUST be encoded as UTCTime and dates in 2050 or later as GeneralizedTime. Both MUST be in Zulu time and include seconds. For UTCTime, a two-digit year of 50 or more means 19YY and less than 50 means 20YY.
sections.eli5: The card lists who it is for, who issued it, its number, and when it starts and stops working. A stamp from the issuer proves nobody changed it.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
Version 3 adds extensions, each with an object identifier, a critical flag and a value. A client MUST reject a certificate that has an unsupported critical extension. The RFC profiles the standard extensions and defines two Internet-specific ones, Authority Information Access and Subject Information Access.

Two extensions matter most for building trust. The key usage extension says what a key may be used for (signature, key encipherment, certificate signing and so on). It MUST appear in certificates whose keys validate signatures on other certificates or CRLs, and when present it SHOULD be marked critical. The basic constraints extension says whether the subject is a CA through the cA boolean, and may limit how deep a certification path can go with pathLenConstraint. It MUST appear as critical in CA certificates whose keys validate certificate signatures. If cA is not asserted, the keyCertSign bit MUST NOT be asserted.

Other extensions cover the key identifiers, certificate policies and policy mappings, subject and issuer alternative names, name constraints, policy constraints, extended key usage, CRL distribution points, inhibit any-policy and freshest CRL.
sections.eli5: Extensions are extra notes on the card, such as 'this card can only be used to sign letters' or 'this holder may hand out cards to others, but only two levels down'.

sections.title: The CRL Profile
sections.content:
A certificate can stop being trustworthy before it expires, for example if the subject changes name, leaves the organization, or the private key is compromised. The X.509 method is for a CA or CRL issuer to periodically publish a signed, time-stamped list of revoked certificates, each identified by serial number. A relying party checks that a certificate's serial number is not on a suitably recent CRL.

The profile requires version 2 CRLs when extensions are used. A CRL has an issuer name, thisUpdate, and nextUpdate, which this profile requires in every CRL. If nothing is revoked, the revoked list MUST be absent. An entry MUST NOT be removed until it appears on one regularly scheduled CRL issued after the certificate's validity period ended. A weakness is that revocation is only as timely as the CRL issue period, which could be an hour, a day or a week.

Delta CRLs carry only updates to earlier revocation information and are flagged by a critical Delta CRL Indicator extension, which can reduce network load. Each revoked entry may carry a reason code, which the RFC says SHOULD be left out rather than use unspecified (0). The profile does not require CRLs at all, because on-line revocation methods defined elsewhere can serve as an alternative.
sections.eli5: When an ID card is lost or stolen, the office posts the card's number on a 'do not accept' list. Shops check the list before trusting a card.

sections.title: Certification Path Validation
sections.content:
Section 6 describes how to decide whether to trust an end entity certificate. The goal is to verify the binding between a subject name and a public key, starting from a trust anchor that is an input to the algorithm. A path of n certificates must satisfy four conditions: the subject of each certificate is the issuer of the next, certificate 1 is issued by the trust anchor, certificate n is the one being validated, and every certificate was valid at the time in question. A self-signed trust anchor certificate is not part of the path. How the path is found is outside the scope of the document.

The algorithm also works out which certificate policies are valid for the path using a valid policy tree, and an application may add more limits. Implementations are required to give the same results as the algorithm but need not use its exact procedure. Some extension steps, such as policy mapping, are optional. Section 6.3 gives a separate procedure for checking certificate status using CRLs.
sections.eli5: To trust a card, follow the chain: each card was signed by the one above it, all the way up to an office you already trust, and none of them have expired.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Certificates and CRLs are digitally signed, so no extra integrity service is needed, and they need not be kept secret. What affects trust is outside the format. The strength of a certificate depends on how the CA and RA verified the subject, so relying parties may want to read the CA's certificate practice statement. The RFC strongly discourages using one key pair for both signing and key management.

Protecting private keys is critical. If a CA's signing key is compromised, an attacker can issue bogus certificates and CRLs, and all certificates issued to that CA MUST be revoked. CAs SHOULD keep secure backups of signing keys. Stale or unavailable revocation information reduces assurance, and relying parties that cannot process critical CRL extensions may miss the newest data. Path validation also depends on trusted CA public keys being distributed through an authenticated out-of-band process, since substituting a key the attacker controls would allow false certificates to be accepted.
sections.eli5: If someone steals the stamp that the ID office uses, they can print fake cards, so guarding that stamp matters most.

items.label: unspecified
items.desc: No reason given; the extension SHOULD be left out instead.

items.label: keyCompromise
items.desc: The subject's private key was compromised.

items.label: cessationOfOperation
items.desc: The operation the certificate was for has ceased.

items.label: removeFromCRL
items.desc: Removes an entry from the list.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PATH CONDITIONS FROM SECTION 6.1

items.title: Chained names
items.text: For every certificate x before the last, the subject of certificate x is the issuer of certificate x+1.

items.title: Anchored start
items.text: Certificate 1 is issued by the trust anchor.

items.title: Target at the end
items.text: Certificate n is the certificate to be validated.

items.title: Valid in time
items.text: Every certificate in the path was valid at the time in question.
